key_terms.meaning: The same operation runs on many pieces of a large dataset at once, each worker on a different slice, with no need for the workers to talk to each other.
One master process splits work into tasks, hands them to many workers, and collects the results; workers never coordinate with each other directly.
Processes that do not share memory exchange data by explicit send and receive calls, so communication is visible in the code.
Several threads inside one process read and write the same memory, so they must use locks or other guards to stay correct.
Running very many independent tasks through a worker pool to maximise completed tasks per hour, not the speed of one task.
A self-contained unit of work with its own inputs and outputs that can be scheduled on any free worker.
A function applied to each input record that emits zero or more key-value pairs; it sees one record at a time.
The framework step that sorts and groups all emitted pairs by key and sends each key's list of values to one reducer.
A function that receives one key and the list of all values emitted for it, and combines them into a smaller result.
Spark's immutable, partitioned collection held in memory across a cluster; a lost partition is recomputed, not replicated blindly.
The recorded chain of transformations that built an RDD, used to recompute a lost partition from the original input.
A virtual machine rented on Amazon Web Services, chosen by instance type (CPU, memory, network) and by Amazon Machine Image.
Object storage on AWS where data sits in buckets as objects reached by a key, with very high durability and no file-system semantics.
A stateful virtual firewall attached to AWS instances that allows or denies traffic by protocol, port and source address.
One running copy of an application started automatically by Google App Engine when request load rises, and stopped when it falls.
An Azure container that holds related resources so they can be deployed, monitored and deleted together.
Software that creates and runs virtual machines on a physical host and controls their access to CPU, memory and devices.
In CloudSim, a simulated task with a length in million instructions and a list of required files, sent to a VM by a broker.
The CloudSim policy object that decides which VM gets which cloudlet; changing the broker changes the scheduling algorithm.
Shortest Job First: the waiting task with the smallest length runs next, giving the lowest average waiting time when lengths are known.

takeaways: A cloud program runs faster or slower mainly because of the parallel model chosen, so match the model to how the work communicates.
High-throughput computing optimises finished tasks per hour across a pool, which is a different goal from making one job finish fast.
MapReduce hides all the hard parts of a distributed job — splitting, shuffling, retrying, failing over — behind two functions you write.
Spark's in-memory RDDs plus lineage-based recovery make iterative algorithms such as PageRank far cheaper than repeated MapReduce jobs.
AWS, Google Cloud and Azure all sell the same four primitives — compute, storage, network, messaging — with different names and different defaults.
Open-source IaaS platforms such as OpenStack turn your own racks into a private cloud with the same API shape as a public one.
CloudSim lets you compare scheduling policies on a laptop before spending money on real virtual machines.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to describe a model or platform and then compare it with an alternative, so always give the mechanism, one worked example and a short comparison table.

bank.q: Explain the three parallel programming models used on the cloud — shared-memory threads, message passing and data parallelism — and state one workload that suits each.
outline: Shared-memory threads: one address space, synchronisation by locks, limited to one machine, suits multicore in-memory work
Message passing: separate address spaces, explicit send/receive, scales to many machines, suits tightly coupled simulations
Data parallelism: same function over many partitions, no inter-worker communication, suits large datasets such as log analysis
Master-worker pattern is the practical form of task-level data parallelism
One concrete example per model with the number of nodes and the failure behaviour

bank.q: Describe the MapReduce programming model: name its phases, explain what the programmer writes and what the framework does.
outline: Input is split into independent chunks; each chunk gets a map task
Map emits intermediate key-value pairs
Shuffle and sort groups all values of the same key
Reduce combines the group into the final output
Framework handles scheduling, data movement, stragglers and retries of failed tasks
Classic word-count example with the pairs emitted for one line

bank.q: Distinguish high-throughput computing from high-performance computing and explain the task-based model used for HTC.
outline: HPC: one large coupled job, low latency is the goal, fast interconnect
HTC: many independent tasks, goal is completed tasks per hour, failures are expected and retried
Task must be self-contained with declared input and output files
Scheduler fills workers, task duration does not matter much
Examples: rendering frames, parameter sweeps, batch record processing

bank.q: List the main AWS building blocks for compute, storage, networking and communication and state the job of each.
outline: EC2 for virtual machines, chosen by instance type and AMI
EBS as network-attached block storage tied to one availability zone
S3 as object storage with buckets and keys
VPC as an isolated virtual network with subnets and route tables
Security groups and network ACLs as firewalls
SQS queues and SNS topics for decoupled communication

bank.q: Write the map and reduce functions for counting how many times each word appears in a large set of documents, and trace one document through the shuffle.
outline: map(doc): for each word emit (word, 1)
Optionally combine locally to cut shuffle volume: (word, partial count)
Shuffle groups all 1s for the same word to one reducer
reduce(word, values): return (word, sum of values)
Trace with a short sample document and show the intermediate pairs
Mention partitioner decides which reducer gets which key

bank.q: An iterative ranking algorithm runs the same matrix multiplication twenty times on a fixed dataset. Explain how you would implement it in Spark and why it beats repeated MapReduce.
outline: Load once, cache the dataset as an RDD or DataFrame in memory
Each iteration is a map plus a reduceByKey or a join, launched by one action
Lineage rebuilds only the lost partition instead of restarting the job
MapReduce would re-read and re-write to disk on every iteration
Quantify: N iterations means roughly N times the disk traffic in MapReduce
Mention checkpointing to cut very long lineages

bank.q: Design a VPC layout for a three-tier web application on AWS with a public web tier, a private application tier and a managed database, listing the subnets, routes and security rules.
outline: VPC with a chosen CIDR block, split into public and private subnets across at least two availability zones
Internet gateway plus route table for the public subnets; NAT gateway for outbound traffic from private subnets
Web tier security group allows 80/443 from the internet
App tier security group allows traffic only from the web tier security group
Database security group allows the database port only from the app tier
Bastion or SSM session for administrative access instead of opening SSH to the world

bank.q: Explain step by step how you would simulate and compare First-Come-First-Served with Shortest Job First in CloudSim for 200 cloudlets on 10 VMs.
outline: Create CloudSim core, datacenter, host and broker objects
Define VM parameters and a VM allocation policy
Create 200 cloudlets with specified lengths and file sizes
Submit cloudlets to the broker through a broker class whose cloudlet-to-VM mapping encodes the policy
Run the simulation and collect start time, finish time and waiting time per cloudlet
Compare average waiting time and makespan for the two policies and explain the SJF advantage

bank.q: Compare Apache Spark with MapReduce on data flow, fault tolerance, latency and cost, and say which you would choose for batch reporting and which for iterative machine learning.
outline: MapReduce: disk between every stage, task-level retry, high per-job overhead
Spark: in-memory RDDs, DAG of stages, pipelined narrow transformations
Fault tolerance: MapReduce re-runs the failed task; Spark recomputes a partition from lineage, with checkpointing for long chains
Shuffle is expensive on both; Spark keeps shuffle output in memory where possible
Iterative and streaming work favours Spark; one-off very large batch jobs still run cheaply on MapReduce-style engines
Shuffle-heavy joins may be memory-bound in Spark, causing spills

bank.q: A startup must host a new application on a public cloud. Compare AWS, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure on compute, storage, networking, scaling model and lock-in, and justify a choice.
outline: Compute: EC2 instances, Compute Engine VMs, Azure Virtual Machines; all offer autoscaling groups
Managed PaaS: App Engine and Cloud Run versus Elastic Beanstalk and App Service
Storage: S3, Cloud Storage, Blob Storage, each with tiers and lifecycle rules
Networking: VPC, VPC, Virtual Network; security groups versus firewall rules
Messaging: SQS/SNS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus and Event Grid
Lock-in comes from managed services and identity, not from virtual machines
Recommendation must be tied to the team's existing skills and the required region

bank.q: Compare the open-source IaaS platforms OpenStack, Eucalyptus and OpenNebula on architecture, API compatibility and the deployment each suits.
outline: Common layer: hypervisor on each host, controller for scheduling, image store, network and block storage services
OpenStack: many cooperating projects (Nova, Neutron, Cinder, Glance, Keystone), open API, heavy to operate
Eucalyptus: built for AWS-compatible APIs, easier to connect to AWS tooling
OpenNebula: smaller, lighter, single-controller design, good for a modest private cloud
All three give self-service portals, quotas and tenant isolation
State the operational cost and skill requirement as part of the comparison

bank.q: Faults are normal at cloud scale. Analyse how shared-memory threads, message passing and master-worker task models each fail, and how each recovers.
outline: Threads on one machine: one crashed thread can corrupt shared state; a machine loss kills all threads together
Message passing: a lost process needs a restart of the whole job unless checkpoints exist
Master-worker: master failure is the single point of failure; worker failure is a simple re-queue of the task
Tasks should be idempotent so re-execution is safe
Stragglers versus failures: speculative execution handles slow workers
CloudSim cannot model these failures, so real testing is needed

bank.q: Evaluate the trade-off between using a managed PaaS such as Google App Engine and raw IaaS virtual machines for a small team deploying a new web application.
outline: PaaS: automatic scaling, patching and monitoring included, faster to first deploy
PaaS: runtime and API constraints, instance startup latency, less control of the network stack
IaaS: full control and portable to another provider, but you own patching, scaling rules and monitoring
Statelessness is required either way when scaling horizontally
Lock-in: PaaS-specific APIs are harder to move than a VM image
Decision rule based on team size, traffic shape and long-term portability needs

glossary.def: Running one job on many processors at the same time so it finishes sooner.
Running a job across several networked machines that share only the network, not memory.
A single sequence of instructions inside a process that shares memory with the other threads of that process.
A bug where the result depends on the unpredictable order in which concurrent threads touch shared data.
A synchronisation point where every participating thread or process must arrive before any may continue.
Work that splits into independent parts with no communication between them, so it scales almost linearly.
A fixed set of processes or machines that repeatedly take tasks from a queue and run them.
The component that decides which task runs on which worker and at what time.
A task that runs far slower than its peers and holds up the whole job.
Launching a duplicate copy of a slow task and taking whichever copy finishes first.
The function that decides which reducer or partition receives a given key after the shuffle.
A local partial reduce run on the same machine as the map, used to shrink the data sent to the shuffle.
The graph of stages Spark builds from a chain of transformations; it has no cycles, so a lost stage can be rebuilt.
A Spark operation such as map or filter that defines a new RDD lazily without computing it.
A Spark operation such as count or save that triggers actual computation of the pending transformations.
A stored template of an operating system and preinstalled software from which new virtual machines are booted.
Storage presented as a raw disk that one machine mounts and formats, such as EBS or a Cinder volume.
Storage where each item is a whole object reached by a key inside a bucket, with no directory tree and no in-place edits.
A separate physical site inside a cloud region, with independent power and network, used for replication.
A logically isolated network inside a public cloud where you choose subnets, routes and firewalls.
Adding or removing instances automatically when a metric such as CPU load crosses a threshold.
One customer of a shared cloud whose resources and data must stay isolated from other customers.
A Java simulation library that models data centres, hosts, VMs, brokers and cloudlets for policy experiments.
